sources.title: Retrieval-augmented generation explained
sources.summary: RAG supplements a language model with an external knowledge base. Its open-book approach can improve the checkability of responses and reduce unsupported claims, but source verification is still required.

sources.title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
sources.summary: RAG combines search or database retrieval with generative language models. Retrieved information is incorporated into the model context to support relevant grounded output.

sources.title: RAG and indexes in Microsoft Foundry
sources.summary: The RAG flow is Retrieve → Augment → Generate. An index organizes information for search; keyword, vector, semantic, and hybrid methods are possible. Embeddings represent content numerically.

sources.title: Retrieval API guide
sources.summary: Semantic search finds related content even with limited keyword overlap. Vector stores function as searchable indexes used for retrieval; a separate model step may synthesize a response.

sources.title: File search guide
sources.focus: Using uploaded documents as a knowledge base
sources.summary: File search uses uploaded files placed in vector stores to retrieve relevant context. File references can connect generated output back to the underlying knowledge base.

sources.title: Design and develop a RAG solution
sources.summary: A document pipeline can split sources into chunks, enrich them with metadata, embed them, and index them. Evaluate retrieval and generated answers independently for groundedness, completeness and relevance.

articles.title: What is RAG?
articles.lead: RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It lets an AI model consult relevant documents before giving an answer.
body: Think of a closed-book exam versus an open-book exam. A normal language model relies mostly on patterns learned during training; a RAG system first looks up relevant material and provides it as context.
RAG does not automatically guarantee truth. It gives the system evidence that can be checked.
articles.takeaway: RAG = search first, then answer with evidence.

articles.title: What problem does RAG solve?
articles.lead: A model may lack recent, private or specialized information.
body: Example: A student asks an AI to explain a specific course policy. The model may not have seen the latest course document.
With RAG, the application can retrieve the course handbook and cite the relevant passage.
articles.takeaway: Use RAG when reliable answers depend on information outside a model’s training.

articles.title: Retrieve → Augment → Generate
articles.lead: Three distinct steps make the answer traceable.
body: Retrieve: Search the knowledge base for passages relevant to the question.
Augment: Add selected passages and their source identifiers to the model prompt.
Generate: Ask the model to explain using those passages; show a citation or admit insufficient evidence.
articles.takeaway: Always retrieve before drafting; verify citations after drafting.

articles.title: Building a searchable knowledge base
body: Select authoritative source documents and record their original URLs.
Create concise, faithful source notes; split longer content into topic-centered chunks.
Attach metadata such as source ID, title, topic and URL. Index the material so it can be searched.
articles.takeaway: Good answers begin with traceable source preparation.

articles.title: Keyword vs semantic search
articles.lead: Matching exact words is not the same as matching meaning.
body: Keyword search is useful for exact phrases and identifiers.
Semantic search can connect similar ideas expressed with different words. Embeddings encode meaning as numerical vectors.
Our static teaching Wiki uses a transparent keyword-based index; it is not a vector database and does not call a live LLM.
articles.takeaway: For this demonstration: a local keyword search; for production: consider semantic or hybrid retrieval.

articles.title: Evidence and citations
articles.lead: Every important slide claim should point back to at least one Wiki source.
body: Keep the source ID attached to each note.
Require at least one relevant citation for each major explanation.
Check whether the cited source actually supports the claim. Citation presence is not the same as citation correctness.
articles.takeaway: Trace a slide claim → Wiki page → source note → original reference.

articles.title: Evaluation and quality checks
articles.lead: Check inputs, retrieval and output—not just the final slide.
body: Source check: Are the URL, publisher and claim valid?
Retrieval check: Did search return relevant Wiki material?
Content check: Are explanations accurate, beginner-friendly and cited?
Presentation check: Do links, keyboard navigation and small screens work?
articles.takeaway: Move checks upstream so a faulty source never reaches the slide.

articles.title: Benefits and limitations
articles.lead: RAG improves access to evidence; it is not a guarantee against hallucination.
body: Benefits: less need to retrain for every new document, easier provenance and more specific answers.
Limitations: bad source material, missing passages or a poor search ranking can still produce bad answers.
A high-quality workflow includes retry paths and an explicit “insufficient evidence” result.
articles.takeaway: RAG helps, but retrieval and verification remain essential.

articles.title: Example: course handbook Q&A
articles.lead: A hypothetical, clearly labeled example of grounded answering.
body: Question: “How many references must my assignment include?”
Retrieve: Find the relevant paragraph in a hypothetical course handbook.
Augment: Attach that paragraph, source title and section to the prompt.
Generate: Answer only if the retrieved handbook explicitly states a number; otherwise explain that the provided evidence is insufficient.
articles.takeaway: Never invent a policy or deadline when the source is missing.

articles.title: Our Wiki-to-slide workflow
articles.lead: Discussion → Ingest 6 sources → Draft Wiki → Retrieve notes → Build slides → Test → Revise.
body: First, define the audience: first-time learners, about 10 minutes.
Next, ingest six traceable, paraphrased source summaries into the Wiki.
Then create an outline and map each slide to at least one Wiki topic and source.
Finally, run source, navigation, text overflow and misconception checks. Retry the failing stage instead of regenerating everything.
articles.takeaway: An early source check and a final link check form the two main quality gates.
